title: The full radio spectrum from ELF to gamma: who uses each band and why
summary: Book-scale tour of the spectrum from ELF through microwave and beyond — who lives in each band and why physics pushed them there.

blocks.title: Every band is a compromise with physics
blocks.body: Frequency is not a fashion choice. Wavelength, antenna size, bandwidth, propagation, and regulation shove services into neighborhoods. This page walks ELF toward light and high-energy radiation so you can see who lives where — and why they cannot casually move.

items.label: Orders of magnitude in one story
Higher carriers can carry fatter pipes — with new pains

nodes.title: ELF
nodes.detail: < 3 Hz–3 kHz (loosely). Users: Submarine / geophysics cues. Note: Huge antennas, tiny bandwidth. Not a ham playground.

nodes.title: VF / voice-freq-ish
nodes.detail: 3–30 kHz. Users: Navigation, some submarine systems. Note: Still enormous wavelengths.

nodes.title: LF
nodes.detail: 30–300 kHz. Users: Time signals, navigation orphans, some experimental. Note: Longwave AM leftovers in a few regions.

nodes.title: MF
nodes.detail: 300 kHz–3 MHz. Users: AM broadcast, NDBs, 160 m ham. Note: Groundwave by day stories; night skip drama.

nodes.title: HF
nodes.detail: 3–30 MHz. Users: Shortwave broadcast, aviation, maritime, ham HF. Note: Ionospheric skip — the classic DX map.

nodes.title: VHF
nodes.detail: 30–300 MHz. Users: FM broadcast, aviation, marine VHF, 2 m / 6 m ham. Note: Line-of-sight plus tropospheric surprises.

nodes.title: UHF
nodes.detail: 300 MHz–3 GHz. Users: TV, cellular, Wi‑Fi edges, 70 cm ham, GPS L1 neighborhood. Note: Handheld antennas; indoor pain; capacity king.

nodes.title: SHF (microwave)
nodes.detail: 3–30 GHz. Users: Satellite, radar, 5G mmWave neighbors, dishes. Note: Beams, rain fade, point-to-point.

nodes.title: EHF
nodes.detail: 30–300 GHz. Users: Backhaul, science, security scanners, research. Note: Atmospheric absorption walls appear.

nodes.title: THz / far-IR edge
nodes.detail: ~300 GHz–3 THz. Users: Labs, imaging research. Note: Not a consumer band — still 'radio' to physicists.

blocks.label: Low frequencies — big antennas, slow pipes

blocks.heading: Why ELF–MF exist at all
blocks.body: At low frequency, wavelengths are enormous. Antennas become landscapes. Data rates crawl. The payoff is penetration and reach: seawater, earth, and beyond-line-of-sight paths that microwave cannot casually copy. If a service lives here, it usually needs physics that higher bands refuse to give.

blocks.heading: HF is a weather system for radio
blocks.body: Between roughly 3 and 30 MHz, the ionosphere can refract signals back to Earth. That makes cheap long-haul links possible — and unreliable. Aviation, maritime, shortwave broadcast, and amateur radio still share this lively, congested commons because satellites and fiber did not erase every need for independent long paths.

More bandwidth until the ionosphere says no

blocks.label: VHF / UHF — line of sight and capacity

blocks.heading: Handhelds, towers, and cellular economics
blocks.body: VHF and UHF shrink antennas into handhelds and cars. Propagation becomes mostly line-of-sight plus clutter. Bandwidth and channelization explode compared with HF, which is why broadcasting, public safety, aviation voice, marine VHF, Wi‑Fi-adjacent services, and much of mobile telephony parked here. Regulation is dense because everyone wants the same real estate.

blocks.label: Microwaves and above — beams, dishes, absorption

blocks.heading: When antennas become optics-adjacent
blocks.body: From a few GHz upward, dishes and phased arrays make narrow beams. Satellite downlinks, radar, point-to-point backhaul, and modern mobile layers live on aiming, noise figures, and atmospheric windows. Rain fade and oxygen/water absorption stop being trivia. Past the traditional radio bands, infrared and optical links continue the communications story with different hardware — and X-rays/gamma remind you the electromagnetic spectrum keeps going long after Wi‑Fi ends.

columns.name: Higher is always better
columns.detail: Ignores penetration, range, and device simplicity. HF and VHF exist for reasons silicon marketing slides forget.

columns.name: Lower is always more 'real radio'
columns.detail: Ignores capacity and antenna physics. Your phone is not a moral failure for living in UHF/GHz.

blocks.heading: Placement check
blocks.prompt: A handheld voice radio for hikers that must work without satellites most often lives in…
blocks.explanation: Portable antennas and local/repeater LOS culture put hikers' radios in VHF/UHF. ELF is absurd for handhelds; X-ray is not a voice band.

blocks.heading: Curiosity next step
blocks.body: Pick one service you use daily (FM, GNSS, Wi‑Fi, LTE/5G). Find its band and name the physics tax it pays. That single hop makes the whole map stick.
